title: First bloom: increased consumer choice after eighteen months of the DMA
method: structured qualitative assessment of compliance changes and open non-compliance issues (submission to the Commission's DMA review consultation)
outcomes: consumer choice (browser choice screen, default apps, NFC payments, account creation); enforcement gaps
headline: Identifies four concrete consumer benefits after 18 months (iOS browser choice screen, default-app choice on iOS, contactless payments without Apple Pay, Google account without Gmail) while listing ongoing suspected non-compliance.
summary_plain: Europe's consumer federation says the DMA has already given people more choice on their phones and Google accounts, but that enforcement against the big platforms must get tougher.
quality: Qualitative stocktake without quantitative outcome data; author campaigns for strong DMA enforcement.

authors: Richard Feasey, Giorgio Monti, Alexandre de Streel (CERRE)
title: Assessing and Improving the DMA's Impact (Issue Paper, DMA@2: Towards Stronger Governance and Evaluation?)
method: review of available evidence (compliance reports, Commission annual reports, ad hoc studies) plus interviews with gatekeepers and business users; proposes evaluation framework
outcomes: quality of evidence on DMA impact; evaluation framework and output indicators
headline: Concludes that gatekeeper compliance reports, Commission annual reports and ad hoc studies to date 'do not provide a good basis for understanding the impact of the DMA' and urges mandatory gatekeeper data reporting.
summary_plain: Brussels think tank finds there is still too little data to say what the DMA has achieved, and proposes the Commission force gatekeepers to collect and report the data needed.
quality: Mainly an evaluation-design paper with interview input; no new quantitative estimates.
interested_party: Project supported by CERRE members including Amazon, Apple, Google, DuckDuckGo, Mozilla, Qualcomm and regulators (ACM, Arcep, EETT)

authors: Fiona Scott Morton, Alissa Cooper, Jacques Crémer, Amelia Fletcher, Paul Heidhues, Giorgio Monti, Rupprecht Podszun, Alexandre de Streel, Tracy Xu
title: Comments on the First Review of the Digital Markets Act
venue: Yale Tobin Center for Economic Policy, February 2026
method: structured expert assessment of the state of DMA enforcement and compliance as of end-2025, with list of enforcement actions and their results
outcomes: enforcement actions and outcomes; compliance challenges; recommendations
headline: Reviews DMA enforcement actions and results to end-2025 and notes a broadly shared assessment that compliance reports alone are insufficient, recommending changes for the 2026 review.
summary_plain: A group of economists and lawyers takes stock of what DMA enforcement has achieved by the end of 2025 and lists where it falls short.
quality: Expert synthesis by a university policy centre; descriptive, no causal estimates; several authors also wrote other DMA pieces.
interested_party: Authors include prominent advocates of digital platform regulation

title: The Digital Markets Act: What Have We Learned after the First Years of Its Application?
method: legal-qualitative review of Commission practice, case law and observable market effects
outcomes: clarity of DMA concepts; practical impact; consumer digital rights
headline: Asks whether the DMA has had measurable market effects and evaluates its practical impact in the light of Commission practice and case law (abstract does not report numbers).
summary_plain: A Czech law professor reviews the first years of the DMA to see whether it has changed markets and improved consumers' digital rights.
quality: Mostly legal analysis with qualitative impact discussion; low weight as empirical evidence.

title: NIS2 Transposition Overview (29 January 2025)
method: survey of national trade association members plus desk research on transposition status in 27 Member States
outcomes: transposition status; national divergences; companies in scope
headline: About three months after the October 2024 deadline only nine Member States had adopted NIS2 transposition laws (BE, HR, GR, HU, IT, LV, LT, RO, SK), with a 'real risk of fragmentation'.
summary_plain: An industry body counted how many EU countries had written NIS2 into national law by early 2025 and found most had not.
quality: Snapshot of legal status, non-exhaustive; not a measure of security outcomes.
interested_party: Trade association of digital industry (subject to NIS2)

authors: European Cyber Security Organisation (ECSO), Working Group Cyber Threat Management
title: White Paper: NIS2 Implementation: Challenges and Priorities
method: survey of 155 cybersecurity practitioners (mostly CISOs) in 23 countries, transposition comparison and sector case studies
outcomes: budget allocation, management engagement, implementation challenges
headline: Only about 28% of surveyed organisations had allocated dedicated budget for NIS2 implementation and 34% reported no management involvement.
summary_plain: A survey of cybersecurity managers found most firms had not set aside money for NIS2 and a third had no board involvement yet.
quality: Convenience sample of 155 respondents, mostly large firms; the paper gives both ~75% and 72% for 'no dedicated budget'.
interested_party: Cybersecurity industry association (members sell compliance products/services)

title: The CyberSmart NIS2 Survey: Key findings on EU & UK readiness
method: survey of 670 business leaders of in-scope smaller firms (50-249 employees), MSPs and UK firms trading with the EU in 9 countries
headline: Just 16% (108 of 670) of in-scope respondents were confident their organisation is fully compliant with NIS2; budget constraints and lack of guidance were the main barriers.
summary_plain: A survey of medium-sized firms found only about one in six think they fully meet NIS2 rules, mostly blaming cost and unclear guidance.
period_geography: UK, PL, NL, IE, FR, DE, IT, DK, BE; late 2025
quality: Vendor survey with self-reported compliance; sample frame not random; includes UK firms.

authors: Mark Child, Ralf Helkenberg (IDC), sponsored by Microsoft
title: Preparing for NIS2 and Beyond: The Next Phase of Cyber Resilience in EMEA
method: two-wave survey (2024 and 2025) of 2,000 organisations with maturity-tier segmentation
outcomes: NIS2 readiness, board engagement, budgets, guidance from authorities
headline: 17.5% of organisations say they are already NIS2-compliant and a further 67.4% expect to be within 12 months; the share in the bottom two maturity tiers fell between 2024 and 2025, though over 1 in 5 still lack clear guidance from national authorities.
summary_plain: A large repeated survey finds European organisations got noticeably better prepared for NIS2 between 2024 and 2025, but few are fully compliant yet.

authors: European Innovation Council and SMEs Executive Agency (EISMEA)
title: EIC Impact Report 2025
method: descriptive monitoring statistics on EIC (Horizon Europe Pillar III) portfolio
outcomes: co-investment, investment rounds, employment and turnover growth, spinouts, innovations
headline: EIC Fund completed over 150 investment rounds under Horizon Europe and attracted over EUR 2.6 billion co-investment (over EUR 3 per EUR 1 invested); EIC-backed firms grow employment and turnover by about 50% within two years of award.
summary_plain: The EU's innovation agency reports that the start-ups it backs under Horizon Europe attracted large private co-investment and grew quickly after funding.
quality: Self-reported monitoring, no counterfactual (growth figures not causal).
interested_party: Commission agency reporting on its own programme

authors: Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM, Netherlands)
title: Position paper DGA
venue: ACM, contribution to the 2025 DGA evaluation
method: structured qualitative assessment from the national competent authority's supervisory experience
outcomes: workability of data intermediation rules; burden on providers; cooperation between authorities
headline: National supervisor finds the DGA's requirements for data intermediation services (Art. 12 a, b, e) 'prohibitively strict' for a mostly start-up, subsidy-dependent market and the provider definition too broad and unclear.
summary_plain: The Dutch regulator that applies the Data Governance Act says its rules for data-sharing intermediaries are too strict and unclear for the small, young firms in this market.
quality: Qualitative supervisory assessment; no counts of registrations or quantitative outcomes.

title: Overview of all AI Act National Implementation Plans (last update 17 June 2026)
venue: EU Artificial Intelligence Act website (Future of Life Institute)
method: tracker of national authority designations across EU-27 based on public sources
outcomes: designation of market surveillance and notifying authorities; fundamental-rights authorities
headline: Many Member States missed the 2 August 2025 deadline: as of June 2026 only 9 had clearly designated national competent authorities, 12 had partial clarity and 6 had none, while all 27 had named fundamental-rights authorities.
summary_plain: A tracker of national AI Act enforcement bodies shows that, nearly a year after the deadline, most EU countries had not fully set up the authorities that will enforce the law.
quality: Desk-based tracker, continuously updated; dependent on public information.
interested_party: Non-profit campaigning for AI safety regulation

title: Deloitte AI Act Survey (Umfrage zum EU AI Act)
method: survey of 500 managers responsible for AI in German companies, 24 July - 14 August 2024
outcomes: preparation for AI Act; perceived effect on innovation
headline: 52% of AI managers expect the AI Act to restrict their innovation (19% expect it to strengthen it) and only about a quarter of firms had started preparing for implementation.
summary_plain: A survey of German company AI managers just after the AI Act took effect found half expected it to hold back innovation and few had started preparing.
quality: Self-reported expectations soon after entry into force; margin of error 8.5-8.7 pp; primary PDF could not be opened (redirect loop).
interested_party: Consultancy selling AI Act compliance services

authors: European Economic and Social Committee (rapporteur Antje Gerstein, co-rapporteur Anastasis Yiapanis)
title: Evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 on market surveillance and compliance of products (information report INT/1106)
method: fact-finding visits with semi-structured interviews in France, Germany, Greece and Malta plus questionnaire of 23 organisations (Jan-Feb 2026)
outcomes: relevance and effectiveness of the MSR; authorised representatives; resources; online sales
headline: Stakeholders rate the MSR highly relevant but only partially effective, citing weak verification of authorised representatives, understaffed authorities and online non-compliance (e.g. a French authority reported over 60% of toys sold online unsafe versus 10-15% offline).
summary_plain: An EU advisory body asked authorities and stakeholders in four countries how the market surveillance rules work and heard that they are sound in principle but under-resourced and weak against online sellers from outside the EU.
period_geography: FR, DE, GR, MT; July 2021 - early 2026
quality: Small qualitative sample (23 questionnaire responses, 4 country visits); perception-based.

authors: Euroconsumers / Test Achats-Test Aankoop (with German and Danish partners)
title: Systemic failures in product compliance on TEMU and Shein
method: mystery shopping and accredited laboratory testing of 162 products (81 per platform) across children's products, USB chargers and jewellery
outcomes: product compliance and safety of goods sold on online marketplaces
headline: 26 of 27 children's products from Temu and all 27 from Shein were non-compliant, and only 1 of 27 Temu chargers fully complied; overall almost two thirds of Temu and 73% of Shein products failed at least one requirement.
summary_plain: Consumer testers bought products on Temu and Shein and found most toys and chargers broke EU safety or labelling rules.
quality: Small, category-targeted sample; measures market outcome the MSR (and GPSR/DSA) target, not the MSR's causal effect.
interested_party: Consumer organisations campaigning on marketplace enforcement

authors: Bundesregierung (BMUV); external evaluation by AFC Public Services GmbH (O. Strecker, W. Voit)
title: Bericht über die Anwendung des EU-Verbraucherschutzdurchführungsgesetzes durch Bundesbehörden (with AFC final evaluation report)
method: external evaluation: case-statistics analysis of CPC requests 2007-2021, 31 stakeholder interviews, online survey and workshop
outcomes: CPC information and enforcement requests, alerts, procedures and outcomes in Germany
headline: Germany handled 382 CPC enforcement requests in 2007-2021 (about 25 a year); the evaluation finds the national CPC implementation effective, with early hearings by the Federal Environment Agency often ending infringements quickly.
summary_plain: Germany's government had its handling of EU cross-border consumer enforcement evaluated and found the system works, with many cases settled quickly once companies are contacted.
quality: Descriptive national evaluation spanning both the 2006 and 2017 CPC Regulations; ministry assessing its own law.
interested_party: Ministry evaluating its own implementation (contracted external evaluator)

title: An unfinished journey: Consumer groups' experience of CPC external alerts two years on
method: case-based assessment of BEUC's four CPC external alerts filed since 2020
outcomes: outcomes and procedure of external alerts under the CPC Regulation
headline: BEUC used the new external-alert tool four times in two years; its airline alert led to commitments from 16 airlines, but transparency and speed of follow-up remain weak.
summary_plain: The EU consumer federation reviews how the new right to alert enforcement authorities worked in practice: it brought results such as airline refund commitments, but slowly and opaquely.
quality: Case evidence from the organisation's own alerts; self-interested assessment.
interested_party: Campaigning consumer organisation; user of the mechanism it evaluates; EU co-funded

searched: searched: 3 WebSearch queries (BEUC/ECIPE/Copenhagen Economics/CEPS geo-blocking assessment; post-2018 empirical geo-blocking studies; BEUC geo-blocking evaluation 2025; Commission 2026 evaluation report). Only items already listed (Alaveras et al., Copenhagen Economics 2024, ECA 2025) or theory papers found; a Croatian conference paper (CROSBI 1047095) could not be opened.

searched: 3 WebSearch queries (Bruegel/CEPS/Delors/Counter Balance/Eurodad InvestEU assessment; ECA special report InvestEU 2025-26; Counter Balance InvestEU fossil analysis). Only the Commission interim evaluation and EFSI ECA report (both already listed) and pre-InvestEU NGO work on EFSI found.

searched: 1 WebSearch query (PLD 2024/2853 company preparedness survey, insurance premiums, transposition). Only law-firm explainers; the directive applies from December 2026, so no ex-post evidence exists yet.
